<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file is safe for the `makepkg --printsrcinfo` gate. At the top-level/global scope, the file contains only standard variable assignments (`pkgname`, `pkgver`, `pkgrel`, `pkgdesc`, `arch`, `url`, `license`, `depends`, `makedepends`, `source`, `sha512sums`, `b2sums`) and function definitions (`prepare()`, `build()`, `package()`). None of these involve command substitution, network requests, downloads, `eval`, or any other executable code that would run during sourcing. The `source` array references the package's own upstream repository (`https://github.com/strongtz/edl-ng`) via a git tag, which is standard AUR practice. The checksums are provided (not SKIP), but this is irrelevant to the `--printsrcinfo` gate since no sources are downloaded or verified at this step.

The `prepare()`, `build()`, and `package()` functions contain operations like `sed`, `dotnet publish`, `install`, `cp`, `chmod`, and `ln`, but these will NOT execute during `makepkg --printsrcinfo` — they are only invoked during later build/package steps, which are out of scope for this narrow safety gate and will be audited in the full PKGBUILD review.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
No executable code at top level; safe for printsrcinfo gate.</summary>
</security_assessment>

<details>
The PKGBUILD file is a standard AUR build script for the edl-ng package. It follows conventional packaging practices without any signs of compromise. The source is correctly specified as a Git repository pointing to the official upstream (strongtz/edl-ng) at the tagged release v1.6.0. The build process uses standard dotnet CLI commands to publish the QCEDL.CLI library, which is appropriate for a .NET-based project. The package installation steps are typical: copying built artifacts to the usr directory, creating symbolic links, and setting proper permissions. There are no network requests to untrusted external hosts, no obfuscated or encoded commands, and no attempts to execute arbitrary code or modify system files outside the package scope. All operations are confined to the package's intended functionality—building and installing its own binaries. The use of environment variables to disable telemetry is a standard privacy-conscious practice and does not indicate a security issue.

No indicators of supply chain attacks, backdoors, or unauthorized modifications were found. The file contains only legitimate build and installation logic consistent with how AUR packages are normally structured.
</details>
